subject: Environment
topic: Paris Agreement and climate negotiations — mixed tiers
description: UNFCCC, Kyoto vs Paris, NDCs, India's targets, COPs, Loss & Damage Fund

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement was adopted at the COP-21 of the UNFCCC in:

options.option_text: December 2014
December 2015 (entered into force 4 November 2016)
December 2009 (Copenhagen)
December 1997 (Kyoto)

questions.explanation: Paris Agreement — adopted 12 December 2015 at COP-21 in Paris. 196 parties. Entered into force 4 November 2016 (after threshold of 55 countries representing 55% of global emissions ratified). Aims — limit global warming to 'well below 2 °C' above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to limit to 1.5 °C. Each country submits voluntary NDCs (Nationally Determined Contributions); ratchet mechanism every 5 years. India ratified on 2 October 2016 (Gandhi Jayanti).

questions.stem: Paris Agreement's main difference from the Kyoto Protocol (1997) is that:

options.option_text: Paris is non-binding for all countries
Paris uses voluntary NDCs from ALL countries (developed + developing); Kyoto bound only Annex-I (developed) countries
Kyoto was about ozone, not climate
Paris has no review mechanism

questions.explanation: Kyoto Protocol (adopted 1997, in force 2005) — top-down legally binding emission targets only on Annex-I countries (developed). Lacked US (Senate refused) — toothless. Paris Agreement — bottom-up voluntary NDCs from EVERY party. Legally binding to SUBMIT NDCs (procedural) but the targets themselves are not legally enforceable. Includes ratchet — strengthen NDCs every 5 years; Global Stocktake every 5 years (first one concluded at COP-28, 2023). 1.5 °C goal added in 2018 IPCC SR15 → reinforced at Glasgow COP-26.

questions.stem: Under its updated NDCs (August 2022), India aims to achieve net-zero by which year?

options.option_text: 2070 (announced by PM Modi at COP-26 Glasgow, 2021)

questions.explanation: Net-zero target year — 2070 (announced at COP-26 Glasgow, 1 November 2021 by PM Modi as part of 'Panchamrit'). The other 4 commitments: (1) reach 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030; (2) 50% of electricity from renewables by 2030; (3) reduce projected CO₂ emissions by 1 billion tonnes by 2030; (4) reduce emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030 (revised from 33-35%). Compare global net-zero targets — China 2060, USA 2050, EU 2050. India's later target reflects 'historical emissions equity'.

questions.stem: The Loss and Damage Fund — to compensate developing countries for irreversible climate harm — was operationalised at:

options.option_text: COP-26, Glasgow 2021
COP-28, Dubai 2023
COP-25, Madrid 2019
Earth Summit, Rio 1992

questions.explanation: L&D Fund — first agreed in principle at COP-27 (Sharm el-Sheikh, 2022) — historic decision after 30 years of demands by Vulnerable countries (V20, AOSIS). OPERATIONALISED at COP-28 (Dubai, December 2023) with initial pledges of ~$700M (UAE, Germany, EU, UK, US contributors). Hosted by World Bank as 'interim' arrangement. India + Pakistan + others demand additionality (not just rebadged climate aid). COP-28 also concluded the first Global Stocktake — finding the world is 'far off track' for 1.5 °C.

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement targets to limit global warming to:

options.option_text: 0.5 °C above pre-industrial levels
Well below 2 °C, with effort to limit to 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels
Below 5 °C
Same as 1900 level

questions.explanation: Article 2 of the Paris Agreement — keep 'well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5 °C'. Pre-industrial baseline = average of 1850-1900. Current warming (~2024) — ~1.3 °C above pre-industrial. The 1.5 °C threshold may be temporarily breached on annual basis as early as 2025-2026 (a single year — different from the long-term 20-year average that the Paris target uses). IPCC AR6 (2021-23) — current pace insufficient.

questions.stem: The 'Common but Differentiated Responsibilities' (CBDR) principle — central to the UNFCCC — recognises that:

options.option_text: All countries have equal responsibility
Developed countries (Annex-I) bear greater historical responsibility and must take the lead in climate action and finance
Only the largest emitters need to act
Climate is a regional, not global, issue

questions.explanation: CBDR — formally CBDR-RC (Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities). Codified in 1992 Rio UNFCCC. Acknowledges that while climate change is a common concern, developed countries (which industrialised first, releasing most cumulative emissions) bear greater obligation. India regularly invokes CBDR + 'climate justice' + 'equitable carbon space'. $100B/year climate finance pledge (Copenhagen 2009) — was meant to operationalise CBDR; still under-delivered.

questions.stem: The 'International Solar Alliance' (ISA) — initiated jointly by India and France — was launched at:

options.option_text: COP-26 Glasgow 2021
COP-21 Paris 2015 — by PM Modi and President Hollande
G20 Bali 2022

questions.explanation: ISA — co-initiated by India and France on 30 November 2015 at COP-21 Paris. Treaty-based intergovernmental organisation (only the 2nd HQed in India after the South Asian University). HQ at Gurugram, Haryana (the Solar Energy Centre). Open to all UN member states. Aim: deploy 1 TW of solar by 2030, mobilise USD 1 trillion of investment, training, R&D. India became the first signatory; the Framework Agreement opened for signature 15 November 2016. As of 2024 — 100+ member countries.

questions.stem: Which US President formally rejoined the Paris Agreement in 2021, making climate re-entry his administration's very first executive action on Day 1 of office?

options.option_text: Donald Trump, who reversed course after the 2020 election results
Joe Biden, signing the re-entry executive order on 20 January 2021
Barack Obama, who had originally signed and ratified the accord in 2016
George W. Bush, following bipartisan Senate pressure on climate policy

questions.explanation: Biden signed the executive order to rejoin the Paris Agreement on 20 January 2021 (Day 1); the US formally re-entered on 19 February 2021 after the mandatory 30-day notification period. Trump is wrong because it was Trump who initiated the withdrawal in 2017 — he never reversed it. Obama signed the original agreement in 2016 but did not rejoin anything in 2021.

questions.stem: Under the Paris Agreement, countries must submit updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) on a fixed cycle, each reflecting greater ambition than the last. What is that cycle?

options.option_text: Annually, so that real-time tracking of emissions progress is possible
Every 5 years, each successive NDC required to reflect greater ambition than the last
Every 10 years, aligned with long-term national low-carbon development plans
Every 3 years, matching the UNFCCC standard review and reporting schedule

questions.explanation: Article 4 of the Paris Agreement mandates NDC updates every 5 years under the 'ratchet mechanism', with each new submission required to represent a progression in ambition beyond the previous one. The 10-year option is a popular distractor — while some countries initially set 2030 targets, the mandatory renewal cycle is 5 years, not 10. There is no 3-year UNFCCC reporting cycle for NDCs.

questions.stem: Under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, 'Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes' (ITMOs) are best described as:

options.option_text: Adaptation grants that developed countries transfer to climate-vulnerable nations
Emission reductions or removals transferred between countries via cooperative approaches
Technology packages that developed nations must freely provide to developing countries
Domestic mitigation units counted unilaterally in a single country's NDC inventory

questions.explanation: ITMOs under Article 6.2 are units representing greenhouse gas reductions or removals that one country transfers to another through bilateral or multilateral cooperative arrangements; the receiving country may apply them toward its own NDC. They are not adaptation grants — those flow via the Adaptation Fund or GCF — and they are by definition cross-border, making the 'unilateral domestic units' option (D) a direct contradiction of what ITMOs are.

questions.stem: The 'Paris Rulebook' — the detailed operational guidelines governing how countries implement the Paris Agreement — was substantially finalised at which Conference of Parties (COP)?

options.option_text: COP23 in Bonn, Germany (November 2017), chaired by Fiji's COP presidency
COP24 in Katowice, Poland (December 2018), covering transparency and NDC accounting rules
COP25 in Madrid, Spain (December 2019), focused on voluntary carbon market rules
COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland (November 2021), finalising the Article 6 framework

questions.explanation: COP24 (Katowice, December 2018) adopted the Katowice Climate Package — the Paris Rulebook — which set rules on enhanced transparency, NDC accounting, adaptation communications, and the global stocktake. The common distractor is COP26 (Glasgow), which finalised only the outstanding Article 6 (carbon markets) provisions; the rest of the Rulebook had been agreed two years earlier at Katowice. COP23 produced preparatory negotiating texts, not the finalised rulebook.

questions.stem: The first 'Global Stocktake' (GST) under the Paris Agreement — a periodic, comprehensive review of collective climate progress designed to inform the next round of NDCs — concluded at which COP?

options.option_text: COP26 in Glasgow (2021), prompting enhanced 2030 commitments from major emitters
COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh (2022), alongside the Loss and Damage Fund decision
COP28 in Dubai (2023), with findings meant to guide NDCs due for submission by 2025
COP29 in Baku (2024), completing the full five-year review cycle from the 2019 baseline

questions.explanation: The first GST was mandated to conclude in 2023 and was formally completed at COP28 in Dubai (December 2023). Its synthesis report found the world was not on track for 1.5 °C and called on countries to submit more ambitious NDCs by February 2025. COP27 is frequently confused with this milestone because it established the Loss and Damage Fund — a separate but equally significant outcome. COP26 focused on finalising Article 6 and the Glasgow Climate Pact, not the GST.

questions.stem: Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement establishes a centralised carbon crediting mechanism regarded as the CDM's successor. Which statement correctly distinguishes Article 6.4 from the Kyoto Protocol's Clean Development Mechanism (CDM)?

options.option_text: Both mechanisms are identical; Article 6.4 simply rebrands CDM under a new name
CDM had no formal UN supervisory body; Article 6.4 creates one under the Paris Agreement
CDM limited hosting to non-Annex I nations only; Article 6.4 extends it to all parties
CDM had a 5% levy directed to the Adaptation Fund; Article 6.4 raised this share to 50%

questions.explanation: Under the CDM, only non-Annex I (developing) countries could host emission-reduction projects; Annex I (developed) countries invested in those projects and received Certified Emission Reductions. Article 6.4 removes this restriction — any party to the Paris Agreement may host a mechanism activity. Option B is wrong because the CDM did have an Executive Board (a formal supervisory body) under the UNFCCC. Option D fabricates a 50% levy — Article 6.6 imposes a 5% levy on Article 6.4 credits for the Adaptation Fund, comparable to the CDM's own levy; 50% is entirely invented.

questions.stem: The Paris Agreement's accounting rules require a 'corresponding adjustment' to prevent double-counting of emission reductions across countries' NDCs. In which scenario is a corresponding adjustment MANDATORY?

options.option_text: A country imposes a domestic carbon tax that cuts its own emissions below its NDC target
A country transfers ITMOs to a second country, which then counts them toward its own NDC
A country receives GCF adaptation finance without selling or transferring any credits
A country voluntarily cancels domestic carbon credits without any cross-border transaction

questions.explanation: A corresponding adjustment is triggered when ITMOs cross borders and are applied toward a recipient country's NDC: the selling country must subtract (adjust downward) those units from its own accounting so the same emission reduction is not claimed by both parties. A domestic carbon tax (A) involves no transfer — the reductions stay within the seller's own NDC boundary. Adaptation finance receipt (C) is not a mitigation transfer at all. Voluntary domestic cancellation (D) retires units permanently without any second country counting them, so no double-counting risk exists.
